analysis.one_liner: Repeals the statutory authority for indefinite military detention of suspected terrorists without trial.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the military detention provision of the 2012 defense law never received a committee hearing or a House vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2012 National Defense Authorization Act included section 1021, which put into law the President's power to have the Armed Forces detain people connected to al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or the September 11 attacks, holding them 'pending disposition under the law of war.' Ron Paul's bill would have deleted that section entirely, eliminating the express statutory basis for holding detainees without criminal charges. It was referred to two committees and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone the government might seek to detain under this authority, including U.S. citizens, who would regain the ordinary requirement that the government charge them with a crime and give them a trial rather than hold them under military custody.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of military detention

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 1021 of the FY2012 NDAA, removing the statutory affirmation that the President's post-9/11 military force authority includes detaining people who substantially supported al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or associated forces [S2][S3].
Repeal would leave detention questions to existing law and courts, rather than an express congressional endorsement of military custody 'pending disposition under the law of war' [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The executive branch and the military would lose an express statutory basis for long-term detention of suspected terrorists without trial, which supporters of section 1021 argued was needed to handle enemy fighters captured in the war on terrorism.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of section 1021 argued it largely restated detention authority the President already claimed under the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force, so repeal would be mostly symbolic and could strip useful statutory clarity about how enemy fighters are handled [S2].

Repeal would not itself free any detainee or bar any other legal basis for detention, so the bill's practical effect depends on what courts and future presidents do with the remaining 2001 war authorization [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For anyone who worries about indefinite detention reaching citizens or green-card holders, repeal removes an express statutory green light for military custody without trial, which is a meaningful civil-liberties gain. The honest counterargument is that the underlying detention claim rests on the 2001 war authorization regardless, so the bill changes the written record of Congress's position more than the immediate facts on the ground.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Armed Services and Foreign Affairs committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended without any hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Ron Paul introduced H.R. 3785 on January 18, 2012 to repeal section 1021 of the FY2012 NDAA, the provision affirming military detention authority over people connected to al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or the September 11 attacks [S1][S2][S3].
Seven members cosponsored the bill, six Republicans and one Democrat [S4].
The bill was referred to the Foreign Affairs and Armed Services committees on introduction; the action history shows no further activity of any kind for the rest of the Congress [S5].
Section 1021 remained in effect, having been signed into law as part of the FY2012 defense authorization, Public Law 112-81 [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch and the congressional defense committees kept the detention authority intact without ever having to defend it in a recorded vote, and no member ever had to go on the record on the repeal.

for.name: Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill repealing section 1021 and delivered introductory remarks on it [S1][S5].

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the NDAA
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record [S5].

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record [S5].

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the 112th House
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; the record shows the bill was referred to two committees and never scheduled for a vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure party lines; the bill's sponsors were 6 Republicans and 1 Democrat, and the record shows no stated opposition from any member [S4].

industries.industry: The executive branch and military (holders of detention authority)
industries.note: Section 1021 locks in the government's express statutory basis to hold suspected terrorists in military custody without trial, including people who 'substantially supported' enemy forces [S2]. Repeal would have taken that written authorization away; the public's interest in due process runs against the government's interest in keeping it. No commercial industry is materially affected by this bill.
